newsitem.title: UK: Rumbustious Clarke takes UK centre stage this week.
newsitem.headline: Rumbustious Clarke takes UK centre stage this week.

text.p: Rumbustious finance minister Kenneth Clarke, who takes centre stage in British politics with two key parliamentary speeches within 24 hours, has never been one to mince his words.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer was due to face the wrath of Euro-sceptics in his ruling Conservative party with a parliamentary statement on Monday clarifying Britain's approach to negotiations on a single European currency.

Such a statement, a day before Clarke presented his last pre-election budget, is unprecedented -- chancellors normally keep a low public profile in the days before they unveil their financial plans for the coming year.
But the portly 56-year-old relishes confrontation. Before heading the Treasury, he battled with health workers, teachers and police leaders in other top ministerial posts.

Since becoming chancellor in May 1993 after Prime Minister John Major sacked Norman Lamont, his unashamedly pro-European views have meant he has spent almost as much time at odds with Conservative right-wingers as he has with the Labour party.

Far from trying to mollify his Euro-sceptic critics with soothing words in the interests of party unity, Clarke said it would be "complete folly" to rule out British participation in the single currency and "pathetic" if Britain waited to see how monetary union developed before making up its mind.

He has been equally candid about the Conservatives' failure to deliver promised tax cuts after the last election in 1992, warning that voters would be deeply suspicious of tax cuts in Tuesday's budget which could not be sustained.
"Mr Clarke is clearly too honest to be a good politician," economists at NatWest Markets wrote in their budget preview.
That judgment does not do justice to his political skills.
At the Conservative party conference in October, Clarke was expected to receive a mauling from right-wingers angry at his sympathy for a single European currency.
Instead, he won a five-minute standing ovation from delegates despite conspicuously failing to promise tax cuts.
Born into a working-class family in Nottingham on July 2, 1940, Clarke earned a law degree at Cambridge University and entered parliament in 1970.
His first ministerial position was at the Health and Social Security Department in 1982 and in 1985 he was made paymaster general with a seat in the cabinet.

After the 1987 general election, he was made a minister for trade and industry. This was followed by a rapid rise to Health Secretary in 1988, Education Secretary in 1990 and Home Secretary (interior minister) after the 1992 general election.

At the Treasury, Clarke has earned a reputation for sound economic management, presiding over a sustained upturn, with remarkably low inflation by Britain's dismal historical standards and falling unemployment.

Lamont has claimed, however, that he put in place many of the economic policies Clarke has benefited from. Sterling's expulsion from the European currency grid in 1992 also played a large part in Britain's recovery from recession.
A decisive politician, said to be popular with subordinates, Clarke has generally come off better from disagreements with the Bank of England over monetary policy.
Clarke was proved right by subsequent economic data when he rejected central bank governor Eddie George's advice to raise interest rates in the spring of 1995.
In October this year, he confounded market expectations by raising interest rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent to choke off inflationary pressures.

Conventional wisdom is chancellors will not risk upsetting millions of home-owners by raising the cost of borrowing barely six months before a general election -- especially when the ruling party is well behind the opposition in opinion polls.

The chancellor opted for prudence rather than bold vote-grabbing gestures in last year's budget and economists expected him to do the same on Tuesday, despite pressure from Conservative back-benchers anxious to secure re-election.
